taxonomyNote: NatureServe and Crother (2017) spell the species name 'saurita' (spelling corrected by Kraus and Cameron 2016); Animal Diversity Web and the batch use 'sauritus'. NatureServe also lists Great Lakes and Atlantic populations separately.
fieldMarks: Slim, long-tailed striped snake, 46-86 cm, with three white, yellow or greenish stripes on a black or dark-brown ground colour.
Head wider than the neck with large eyes and a light bar in front of each; upper lip scales bright white or yellow without the dark borders of garter snakes.
Belly white, yellow or green and unblotched; scales keeled; females slightly larger than males.
behavior: Fast-moving and diurnal; usually at the edge of water but also in moist meadows; basks on logs and rocks and in bushes.
Active April-October, hibernating in abandoned rodent or crayfish burrows or anthills, sometimes with other snakes.
Eats mainly frogs, salamanders and their larvae plus small fish, taken by stalking or chasing; live-bearing with young 16-24 cm.
habitat: Wet meadows, marshes, seasonally flooded prairies, bogs, pond and lake shores and swamps, in or near sun-exposed vegetation along water's edge; climbs low vegetation.
range: Eastern North America east of the Mississippi River from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Louisiana; in Canada Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia (NatureServe rank N4).

lookalikes.name: Western ribbon snake
lookalikes.howToTell: Western lacks the broad brown ventrolateral stripe and has large paired parietal spots and a longer muzzle and tail (Animal Diversity Web).

lookalikes.name: Garter snakes
lookalikes.howToTell: Garter snakes have dark borders on the upper lip scales, whereas ribbon snake lip scales are plain white or yellow (Animal Diversity Web).
